subject: psychology
topic: You can remember things that never happened
angle: While post-event misinformation and specific techniques like guided imagery can implant false memories, some individuals are less susceptible based on their analytical reasoning and interest levels.
title: The Malleability of Memory

hooks.text: Can you trust your own memories?
You think your memories are facts. They are often reconstructions.
You are letting others rewrite your past.
A chair. A story. A lie you believe is true.

reveal.headline: You can remember things that never happened.
reveal.body: Misinformation can implant rich autobiographical false memories. This effect is stronger when guided imagery or pressure to answer is used.

explain.headline: Memory is not a fixed record.
explain.body: A substantial number of people yield to the misinformation effect even when they have correct memories of the original materials. Social influence may play a role alongside memory failure.

matters.headline: Your history is malleable.
matters.body: That may be why some people are less likely to report false memories. Analytical reasoning and high interest in a topic can reduce your susceptibility to distorted information.

example.headline: A conversation with a friend.
example.body: You sit in a quiet kitchen. You discuss a news story. You tell a detail about a past event that feels real. It never happened.

question.headline: How much of your past is true?

stat.label: reduction of the misinformation effect when post-warnings are used

claims.text: A substantial number of participants yielded to the misinformation effect even though they had correct memory about the original materials.
claims.quote: A substantial number of the participants yielded to the misinformation effect in the memory test even though they had correct memory about the original (and postevent) materials.

claims.text: Guided imagery and pressure to answer make it more likely to implant rich autobiographical false memories than non-directive instructions.
claims.quote: The moderator techniques for implanting false memories revealed a significantly lower probability of implanting false rich memory with non-directive instructions ( d = 0. 90[0. 53, 1. 27]) than with guided imagery ( d = 1. 45[1. 32, 1. 58]), or with pressure to answer ( d = 1. 56[1. 17, 1. 95]) instructions.

claims.text: Post-warnings are surprisingly effective, reducing the misinformation effect to less than half of its size on average.

verdict: The evidence shows that false memories can be successfully implanted or distorted by misinformation, though the extent of this effect varies by individual cognitive traits and the specific methods used.
caveat: The research suggests that some people may give wrong answers even when they correctly remember the original information, indicating that social influence may play a role alongside memory failure.
caption:
Your brain can create memories of events that never occurred.

Research shows that misinformation and guided imagery can implant false autobiographical memories. However, analytical reasoning and high interest levels can reduce this susceptibility. Social influence may also play a role in why people give wrong answers despite remembering the truth.
